test.purpose: A call from one declared scope into another appears as a crossing naming both ends.

test.name: HLR-094: a shared global crossing a boundary is reported too
test.purpose: A scope sharing a variable with another without calling it has not been isolated, and the crossing names the object.

test.name: HLR-094: exactly the two crossings are reported
test.purpose: The count in the heading matches the rows, so neither kind is reported twice nor an intra-scope edge counted.

test.name: HLR-115: with no scopes declared the analysis is omitted with a reason
test.purpose: The heading states the omission rather than leaving an empty table to be read as isolation verified.

test.name: HLR-094: an edge within one scope is not a crossing
test.purpose: The same calls and the same shared variable, with both files in one declared scope, produce nothing.

test.name: HLR-094: a file matching no declaration is outside the partition
test.purpose: A file no declaration names lies outside the partition rather than in a scope of its own.

test.name: HLR-063: a malformed scope declaration is a usage error
test.purpose: A declaration that cannot be parsed ends the run with the fatal status and a diagnostic, rather than becoming a scope matching nothing.

test.name: HLR-032: the state sections survive a record round trip byte-identically
test.purpose: A report regenerated from the saved record is byte-identical to the live one, with the reachability and global-state sections included.

test.name: HLR-032: a global-state finding survives the round trip
test.purpose: The verdict and its participants are carried in the record, and the citation is derived from the verdict on both paths rather than stored.

test.name: HLR-080: Ca and Ce match the hand-computed table
test.purpose: The three components' afferent and efferent couplings and their Instability values match the table worked out by hand in the fixture header.

test.name: HLR-080: a repeated call does not raise efferent coupling
test.purpose: One caller invokes the same component twice. Coupling counts components depended upon, not calls made, so the repeat must not move the figure — without it the fixture would pass against an implementation counting call sites.

test.name: HLR-082: instability is Ce over Ce plus Ca
test.purpose: The bottom layer is depended on by both others and depends on nothing: 0.00, and a real number rather than undefined.

test.name: HLR-082: a component with both couplings zero is undefined, not zero
test.purpose: The division the requirement forbids. Reporting 0.00 there would claim maximum stability for a file with no relationships at all.

test.name: HLR-080: every component appears, not only the interesting ones
test.purpose: The table lists every component rather than only those crossing a threshold, which would make it a finding list.

test.name: HLR-081: no component is a bottleneck at the default threshold
test.purpose: Asserted so the flag has to be earned: a suite that only ever saw a flagged component would pass against an implementation flagging everything.

test.name: HLR-081: a component is a bottleneck when both couplings meet the threshold
test.purpose: Lowering the threshold produces the flag, and the component with zero efferent coupling stays clear — the rule is both couplings, not either.

test.name: HLR-099: the bottleneck threshold is marked as elc's own heuristic
test.purpose: The finding names the threshold as elc's own rather than citing a standard it does not have.

test.name: HLR-081: the threshold is configurable and appears in the heading
test.purpose: The value in force is stated in the report, so a reader knows what the flags were judged against.

test.name: HLR-083: a cycle between two components is reported as an ordered loop
test.purpose: The loop is reported in order and closed, so the reader sees which edge to cut rather than only which files are entangled.

test.name: HLR-083: the same pair is a recursion finding as well
test.purpose: Mutual recursion across two files is legitimately both: one statement says the stack depth has no finite bound, the other that the files cannot be built or understood apart.

test.name: LLR-CYC-03: mutual recursion within one file is NOT a component cycle
test.purpose: The case HLR-083 calls out by name. A file does not depend on itself, so the component projection holds no loop.

test.name: LLR-CYC-03: that same file still reports the recursion
test.purpose: Paired with the test above so that an implementation detecting nothing anywhere cannot pass it.

test.name: HLR-083: an acyclic project reports no cycles
test.purpose: No cycle is invented where none exists.

test.name: HLR-079: a call bypassing an intervening layer is skip-level
test.purpose: A call descending two layers is reported with both endpoints and the layers crossed.

test.name: HLR-118: a call inverting the declared direction is reported separately
test.purpose: A call ascending one layer is reported as a direction inversion, with its own kind.

test.name: LLR-LAY-03: the two are distinct findings, each without the other
test.purpose: One call skips without inverting and the other inverts without skipping. An implementation folding them into a single layering violation fails here, and so does one reporting a skip only when the call also inverts.

test.name: HLR-079: a call descending exactly one layer is not reported
test.purpose: The arrangement the user declared produces nothing, so the findings above have to be earned.

test.name: HLR-079: the layers crossed are reported with the finding
test.purpose: The ordinal distance travels with each finding, since the requirement asks for the layers crossed and not merely that some were.

test.name: HLR-078: the declared order determines the direction
test.purpose: Declaring the same layers bottom-up inverts every judgement: the call that skipped downward now ascends two layers and is both findings, and the one that inverted now descends one and is nothing.

test.name: HLR-078: --stratum-order states the direction explicitly
test.purpose: The order option corrects layers declared in the wrong sequence, and may be given before them.

test.name: HLR-063: --stratum-order naming an undeclared layer is a usage error
test.purpose: A misspelt layer name ends the run rather than silently leaving the layering measured against something else.

test.name: HLR-063: a partial --stratum-order is a usage error
test.purpose: A partial order determines no direction, and silently completing it would invent one.

test.name: HLR-063: a malformed stratum declaration is a usage error
test.purpose: A declaration that cannot be parsed ends the run with the fatal status and a diagnostic.

test.name: HLR-115: with no strata declared the analysis is omitted with a reason
test.purpose: The heading states the omission rather than leaving an empty table to read as a clean architecture.

test.name: LLR-CTR-09: omitting layering does not omit the coupling table
test.purpose: A run with no strata still reports coupling and instability for every component.

test.name: LLR-ARC-04: a stratum matching no component is diagnosed and retained
test.purpose: Retained rather than dropped: dropping it would renumber the layers below and change what the remaining calls are compared against, turning a typo into a wrong answer.

test.name: HLR-094: a component in no declared stratum is outside the partition
test.purpose: With only one layer declared, the calls touching undeclared files produce nothing.

test.name: HLR-032: the architecture sections survive a record round trip
test.purpose: A report regenerated from the saved record is byte-identical to the live one, with the coupling, cycle and layering sections included.

test.name: HLR-032: a cycle and its loop survive the round trip
test.purpose: The ordered loop and the coupling figures come back from the record, neither being recomputable without a graph.

test.name: HLR-162: the back-call index matches the hand-computed value
test.purpose: One inverted call over the six inter-layer call edges the fixture's README counts by hand — 16.67% violating, 83.33% conforming, over 6.

test.name: HLR-163: the skip-call index matches the hand-computed value
test.purpose: One skip-level call over the same six edges, reported the same way and over the same denominator.

test.name: HLR-164: the indices agree with the violation table beside them
test.purpose: The percentages and the rows asserted in one test, over one run. An index disagreeing with the list printed beside it is the failure HLR-164 exists to make impossible, and only an assertion that reads both catches it.

test.name: HLR-163: the two indices are reported apart and never summed
test.purpose: Two rows and no total. The combined figure a reader might expect — 33.33% here — is asserted absent, since summing would double-count exactly the call that both skips and inverts.

test.name: HLR-162: a project with no inter-layer call reports both undefined
test.purpose: Both files in one declared layer: two call edges exist and neither has a direction to invert, so the answer is "nothing demonstrated" rather than "perfectly conformant". Both 100.00% and 0.00% are asserted absent.

test.name: HLR-115: with no strata the conformance section states the omission
test.purpose: With nothing declared the section is a stated omission naming the option that would fill it, rather than an empty table reading as a clean bill of health.

test.name: HLR-165: the matrix over declared layers matches the hand-drawn grid
test.purpose: The whole grid asserted against the one drawn by hand in the fixture's README, rather than a cell at a time — a per-cell assertion passes against a transposed matrix for every symmetric pair.

test.name: HLR-166: the below-diagonal cells account for exactly the back-calls
test.purpose: The sum below the diagonal and the count of inverted rows in the layering table, asserted together over one run. The grid and the list are two views of one fact, and this is where that is pinned end to end.

test.name: HLR-166: subjects run in ascending layer order, not declaration order
test.purpose: `--stratum-order` reverses the declared direction, and the call that was a back-call moves above the diagonal. Ordering by declaration order would put the violations on the wrong side of the grid for every project that uses the option.

test.name: HLR-165: with no strata declared the matrix is over directories
test.purpose: The fallback, over the same six edges arranged by path rather than by layer, with the heading saying which of the two the reader is looking at — since with directories no cell below the diagonal is a violation.

test.name: HLR-161: a component outside every stratum reaches no matrix cell
test.purpose: With only the middle layer declared the grid is one subject wide and holds nothing, the same treatment the layering findings give an undeclared file.

test.name: HLR-166: the convention is printed with every rendering
test.purpose: The aligned table, the Markdown report, and the CSV companion all carry the orientation sentence. A reader who has to infer which way round the grid runs gets the opposite answer half the time.

test.name: HLR-190: the Markdown matrix folds the grid and keeps the convention out
test.purpose: The Markdown rendering of the matrix places the grid behind a disclosure element stating its row count, with the heading and the convention note above the fold — the convention being what makes a cell below the diagonal a back-call rather than a number, for a reader who has not expanded the grid yet. The aligned rendering gains no element and still carries the note.

test.name: HLR-166: the CSV companion carries the grid the report shows
test.purpose: The companion's rows are asserted against the same hand-drawn grid the report is, so the machine-readable copy cannot drift from the printed one.

test.name: HLR-064: a directory carrying a comma is quoted in the CSV matrix
test.purpose: Built in the test's temporary directory rather than committed, since a directory with a comma in its name is awkward to carry in a repository and the escaping rule is what is under test rather than the tree.

test.name: HLR-104: the matrix companion needs a name to derive
test.purpose: Asking for the companion with the report on standard output writes no file and is not an error, and the report still carries the matrix — only the companion needs a path to be named from.

test.name: HLR-086: each boundary value classifies into exactly one band
test.purpose: The three boundaries that produce findings band as the published table says.

test.name: HLR-086: the bands below the warning threshold produce nothing
test.purpose: Five of the eight boundaries are silent. An implementation banding 8 and 10 as warnings would pass the test above and fail this one.

test.name: HLR-086: the acceptable band is silent, not a gap
test.purpose: The 8-10 range produces no finding, which is the band an earlier reading of the thresholds left out.

test.name: HLR-086: exactly three fan-out findings come out of the boundary file
test.purpose: The count catches a band claiming a value twice, which a per-value assertion would not.

test.name: HLR-031: a measurement inside its band is still reported
test.purpose: A fan-out of 10 produces no finding and is still in the fan-out table. The findings list is the subset that crossed a line, never a replacement for the measurements.

test.name: HLR-099: every finding names its source
test.purpose: No finding row is emitted without a source column, and the fan-out rows cite Henry-Kafura.

test.name: HLR-099: recursion is attributed to MISRA C Rule 17.2
test.purpose: The safety standard the recursion finding rests on is named in the report.

test.name: HLR-099: a single-function global is attributed to MISRA C Rule 8.9
test.purpose: The global-state verdict carries a severity and the published rule that draws the line.

test.name: HLR-099: the bottleneck threshold is marked as elc's own
test.purpose: The one threshold that is not a published standard says so where it is read, which is what keeps the no-built-in-opinion claim honest while shipping MISRA and Martin values beside it.

test.name: HLR-099: the label appears on exactly the rows that earn it
test.purpose: The elc-heuristic label appears on exactly the rows entitled to it — the bottleneck, fan-in and maintainability bands — and on no row citing MISRA, Martin, McCabe or Henry-Kafura. Stated as a correspondence rather than an absence, since a report can now legitimately contain the words.

test.name: HLR-084: every dependency cycle is reported at critical severity
test.purpose: The acceptable count of cycles is strictly zero, so each is critical.

test.name: HLR-123: every finding carries a severity from the closed set
test.purpose: No row carries a severity outside info, warning and critical.

test.name: HLR-123: findings are ranked most severe first
test.purpose: Critical rows precede warning rows, because the list exists to be worked from the top.

test.name: HLR-100: severity does not move the exit status
test.purpose: A project reporting critical findings still exits 0 when every file was read. The exit status is reserved for failures; deciding what a finding warrants is the caller's business.

test.name: HLR-100: the summary counts findings without gating on them
test.purpose: The counts are figures to read rather than gates to pass, and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-098: a project inside every band reports no findings
test.purpose: A project whose every measurement sits inside its accepted range produces an empty findings list.

test.name: HLR-031: the empty Findings section is still emitted
test.purpose: The heading appears with nothing under it, because an absent section is indistinguishable from a renderer that forgot.

test.name: HLR-101: no finding proposes a fix
test.purpose: No finding contains imperative remediation text. elc reports where a measurement falls and which standard says so, and stops there.

test.name: HLR-032: findings survive a record round trip byte-identically
test.purpose: A regenerated report is byte-identical to the live one with the findings section included.

test.name: HLR-056: a regenerated report keeps each finding's attribution
test.purpose: The citation cannot be re-derived on regeneration, which has no measurements to band, so the record carries it.

test.name: HLR-085: fan-out is exact at every band boundary
test.purpose: Fan-out is correct for 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15 and 16 distinct callees — the values Phase 12 will band, asserted individually so a failure names the boundary that moved.

test.name: HLR-085: a repeated call does not raise fan-out
test.purpose: Every caller in the fixture invokes one helper twice; the figures are unchanged, which is what the whole boundary table rests on.

test.name: HLR-085: a function that calls nothing has fan-out zero
test.purpose: A leaf reports zero rather than being omitted.

test.name: HLR-085: every function appears, not only the interesting ones
test.purpose: All twenty-four functions are listed: this is a measurement table, not a finding list.

test.name: HLR-156: fan-in counts the distinct functions that call one
test.purpose: The hub reports three callers and each leaf one, from a source where those are the counts.

test.name: HLR-156: a repeated call does not raise fan-in
test.purpose: The hub calls each leaf twice and each leaf's fan-in stays one: fan-in counts callers, not call sites — the distinctness rule fan-out is built on, read backwards.

test.name: HLR-156: a function nothing calls has fan-in zero
test.purpose: An entry point reports zero rather than being omitted. Drawing a conclusion from an absence of callers is the reachability analysis's job, not this measurement's.

test.name: HLR-156: every function reports a fan-in, not only the connected ones
test.purpose: All eight functions are listed: this is a measurement table, not a finding list.

test.name: HLR-183: one function table carries every per-function figure
test.purpose: One table carries the line range, ELOC, complexity, fan-in and fan-out of every function, and neither of the two tables that used to carry the degrees is present. Three tables listing the same functions were three chances to disagree about which functions exist.

test.name: HLR-183: the Henry-Kafura metric is withdrawn, per function and total
test.purpose: No report carries the formula, the ordinal caveat, or a project-level Henry-Kafura figure. The fan-out band keeps the Henry-Kafura attribution, which is a citation for a threshold rather than a metric of its own.

test.name: HLR-085, HLR-156: the degrees are reported as zero, not as blank
test.purpose: A function at either end of the call graph reports its degree as 0, and never as the `undefined` Instability shows where its own inputs vanish — the two tables sit near enough for the substitution to be an easy mistake.

test.name: HLR-188: an empty table is named rather than presented
test.purpose: A fixture with nothing to put in a table presents no heading for it, and names it in the closing statement instead.

test.name: HLR-087: the hand-counted depth matches
test.purpose: The four-layer chain measures four.

test.name: HLR-088: the deepest chain is reported in full, in order
test.purpose: The ordered sequence from entry point to deepest leaf is reported, not merely its length.

test.name: HLR-088: the deepest branch is taken, not the first
test.purpose: The entry point calls the shallow branch first; the reported chain is the deep one, so the traversal is a longest-path search and not a first-path one.

test.name: HLR-087: the depth is presented with the unresolved count
test.purpose: The depth heading states the unresolved count, so the figure is read as the lower bound it is.

test.name: HLR-089: direct and mutual recursion are both reported
test.purpose: One decomposition finds both kinds, and labels which is which.

test.name: HLR-089: the recursive functions are named
test.purpose: The members of each cycle are named, since MISRA C Rule 17.2 is about which functions are involved.

test.name: HLR-090: recursion yields no depth figure, and the run terminates
test.purpose: A recursive graph reports unbounded depth with no chain, and the run completes — a longest-path search over it would not.

test.name: HLR-090: no finite depth is invented for a recursive graph
test.purpose: No layer count appears anywhere in the report for a recursive graph.

test.name: HLR-115: with no entry points, depth is omitted with its reason
test.purpose: The run succeeds and the report states that no entry points were declared, rather than reporting an empty or zero result.

test.name: HLR-115: an omitted depth does not omit the other measurements
test.purpose: Fan-out is still reported when the depth analysis is omitted; omitting one analysis does not silence its neighbours.

test.name: HLR-095: main is not inferred, however obvious it looks
test.purpose: A file containing an obvious entry point still omits the analysis, because entry points are declared and never guessed at.

test.name: HLR-115: an entry point matching nothing is a distinct omission
test.purpose: A declared symbol matching no analysed function produces its own omission message, distinct from having declared none.

test.name: an unmatched entry point is diagnosed on stderr
test.purpose: The unmatched symbol is named on standard error, and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree agree
test.purpose: Two runs produce identical reports.

test.name: HLR-033: the targets may be given in either order
test.purpose: The report does not depend on the order the targets were named in.

test.name: HLR-156, HLR-183: the flow figures survive a record round trip
test.purpose: Both degrees are carried by the record and restored from it, and joined onto the functions they describe. Neither can be recomputed: regeneration has no graph and no source to build one from, so a record carrying fan-out alone would regenerate every fan-in as zero.

test.name: HLR-056: the measurements survive a record round trip
test.purpose: A report regenerated from a record is byte-identical and still carries the depth, since none of the call-tree measurements can be recomputed without the source.

test.name: HLR-102: the emitted call tree renders under Graphviz
test.purpose: Validity is settled by handing the file to Graphviz and requiring it to render, never by matching text that looks like DOT — the first artefact elc produces for another program to read deserves the reader's own verdict.

test.name: HLR-102: the recursive tree renders too
test.purpose: The second tree renders as well, so the annotations only it carries cannot have broken the syntax.

test.name: LLR-STY-02: stripping every annotation leaves the same valid tree
test.purpose: The degradation claim tested by performing the degradation: every attribute is deleted from the file, and what is left must still render and must still hold the same twenty-five nodes and nineteen edges.

test.name: HLR-103: the call tree is written without being asked for
test.purpose: The companion appears with no option naming it, which is the default the requirement states.

test.name: HLR-103: --no-dot suppresses it
test.purpose: The report is still written and the companion is not, so declining the artefact costs the run nothing else.

test.name: HLR-104: no call tree is written when the report goes to stdout
test.purpose: With no output path there is no name to derive, so nothing is written and no default name is invented.

test.name: HLR-104: still none on stdout with generation disabled
test.purpose: "Whether or not generation was disabled" is the requirement's wording, so both routes to the same absence are asserted: the destination decides it, not the switch.

test.name: HLR-119: the companion is named from the report by substitution
test.purpose: An output of analysis.md yields analysis.dot rather than analysis.md.dot, and the companion takes no path of its own.

test.name: HLR-119: the .dot and the GraphML are siblings of one report
test.purpose: Both companions derive from the same output path in one run, which is what makes the naming rule one rule rather than two that happen to agree.

test.name: the tree holds one cluster per source file and every function
test.purpose: Six clusters and twenty-five nodes, matching the hand-worked table: the drawing accounts for every function the report does.

test.name: LLR-DOT-04: nodes are emitted in ascending identifier order
test.purpose: This is the one renderer that walks the graph rather than the sorted report model, so it must impose its own order; without this the graph library's internal enumeration would reach the output.

test.name: LLR-DOT-04: each node's adjacency is in ascending target order
test.purpose: The second half of the same guarantee, on the edges rather than the nodes.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree produce an identical call tree
test.purpose: Byte-identical across runs, which is what the imposed ordering exists to deliver.

test.name: only call edges are drawn; a shared global is not a call
test.purpose: The artefact is the call tree. Two functions joined by a shared global and by nothing else have no edge between them; their coupling reaches the drawing as a property of each node instead.

test.name: HLR-105: the deepest call chain is annotated, nodes and edges
test.purpose: Six functions and the five steps between them. The chain lies inside the accepted band, so it is annotated because it is the chain and not because it warned — which is the case a fixture built only from findings would miss.

test.name: HLR-105: every unreachable function is annotated
test.purpose: All seven, including the four that call one another in a region no path from the entry point enters — reachable and connected are different properties.

test.name: HLR-105: a fan-out over the band is annotated with its severity
test.purpose: Eleven distinct callees is the first value that warns, and the drawing carries the catalogue's severity rather than a view of its own.

test.name: HLR-105: both participants in a hidden channel are annotated
test.purpose: The writer and the reader, neither of which calls the other. HLR-105 asks for the participants, so the annotation is on the functions rather than on an edge.

test.name: HLR-105: two findings on one node ride two attributes
test.purpose: A function that both takes part in a hidden channel and is unreachable shows both, because each annotation takes a different Graphviz attribute. One overwriting the other would make a drawing silently incomplete.

test.name: HLR-105: every member of a dependency cycle is annotated
test.purpose: Both components, not only the one the catalogue files the finding against: a finding has one subject and a set has no single location, and the requirement asks for the members.

test.name: HLR-105: a bottleneck component is annotated and attributed
test.purpose: The coupling finding reaches the cluster, and carries the label marking it as elc's own heuristic rather than a published standard.

test.name: HLR-105: every member of a recursive cycle is annotated
test.purpose: Both mutually recursive functions carry the mark and the finding, for the reason both members of a dependency cycle do.

test.name: HLR-100: a critical annotation does not become an exit status
test.purpose: A run full of critical findings in which every file was read still exits 0. Severity is a label, and drawing it on a graph does not change that.

test.name: a forward declaration is not a node
test.purpose: Three nodes and not four, which also pins that the C module's function query captures definitions rather than declarations.

test.name: LLR-DOT-05: a companion that cannot be written is diagnosed, not fatal
test.purpose: The primary report is the deliverable and the call tree is a companion, so a companion that cannot be created leaves the report written and says so. The path is blocked with a directory rather than with permissions, which fopen refuses whatever the mode is — so the case reproduces for root, where a read-only directory would not.

test.name: HLR-194: the companion is named from the report and written beside it
test.purpose: The companion follows the rule every other companion follows: named from the report's output path, written beside it.

test.name: HLR-119: no companion is written when the report goes to stdout
test.purpose: There is no name to derive one from, so none is written — and that is not a usage error, exactly as for the GraphML export.

test.name: HLR-194: no companion is written without the option
test.purpose: Off unless asked for, like every other companion but the call-tree drawing.

test.name: HLR-194: the companion records the invocation
test.purpose: The first question asked of a log from a machine nobody has is what was actually run.

test.name: HLR-194: every message sent to standard error is in the companion
test.purpose: Every line standard error received appears in the companion — asserted line by line over a run that produces several, rather than by spot-checking one.

test.name: HLR-195: an unparsable region is recorded with its source
test.purpose: The offending construct itself reaches the log, which is the point: a grammar that fails on a construct is debugged from the construct, and that is the one thing a maintainer holding only a bug report does not have.

test.name: HLR-195: a sound file records no parse failure
test.purpose: The converse, which stops the test above passing against an implementation that records a failure for every file.

test.name: HLR-194: standard error is identical with the option and without
test.purpose: The companion records a run and is not a result of one; a diagnostic aid that altered what it observed would be worse than none.

test.name: HLR-194: the report is identical with the option and without
test.purpose: The results stream is untouched by the option, as HLR-038 requires of everything that is not a result.

test.name: HLR-194: the exit status is identical with the option and without
test.purpose: Asking for a debug log neither fails a run nor rescues one.

test.name: HLR-032: the timestamps stay out of the report
test.purpose: A log nobody watched being produced needs timestamps; a report must be byte-identical across two runs over one target. The companion is a record of a run rather than a result of one, and that is the line they sit on.

test.name: HLR-194: the companion is readable while the run is still going
test.purpose: Observed from outside by killing the run and reading what survived. This is the property the companion exists for: a run that faults on a tree nobody can reproduce still leaves everything up to the fault on disk, where a buffered implementation would leave an empty file.

test.name: the hand-counted totals match with no image
test.purpose: Two files, 61 physical lines, five functions and 13 ELOC, against a table worked out by hand in the fixture's README. The unfiltered figures are the baseline every filtered one is read against.

test.name: HLR-140: the image restricts the report to the functions it defines
test.purpose: Three functions and nine ELOC where the source holds five and 13. The two the image lacks contribute to no reported metric.

test.name: HLR-140: a static function reaches .symtab and is retained
test.purpose: A local function is in `.symtab` and not in `.dynsym`, so a reader taking only the dynamic table would report it missing from an image that plainly contains it.

test.name: HLR-153: a region the build excluded is pruned from a kept function
test.purpose: `guarded` survives the link and three statements inside it produced no instruction; the condition that excluded them is one elc cannot decide from the source, so only the image's line information can rule them out. ELOC 7 falls to 4 and the project total 15 to 12.

test.name: HLR-153: a function every build compiles is kept whole
test.purpose: The other direction, and what stops the pruning test passing against an implementation that deleted the file wholesale: the two functions every configuration compiles keep their exact ELOC and all four functions are still reported.

test.name: HLR-154: a file compiled without debug information loses no line
test.purpose: The dangerous case, and it is dangerous because it is silent. The unit contributes no line entries at all, so a rule keyed on absence would find every line of it uncompiled and delete the file — leaving a report that is smaller, internally consistent, and wrong.

test.name: HLR-155: both counts are reported
test.purpose: Three statements and the two directives around them pruned; one file whose coverage could not be established. The pair is read as the unresolved-call count and the undecided-region count are — the first states what the filter removed, the second where it could not look.

test.name: HLR-133: the region is undecided, so only the image ruled it out
test.purpose: The fixture's whole assertion rests on this. Were the condition decidable from the source, Phase 15 would have removed the region before the image was consulted and every pruning test would pass against an implementation that read no debug information at all.

test.name: HLR-153: an image without debug information prunes nothing
test.purpose: HLR-141 forbids *requiring* debug information, so its absence costs the finer granularity and nothing else: every ELOC figure is the unfiltered one, nothing is pruned, and both files are counted uncovered rather than silently emptied.

test.name: HLR-153: the metrics without debug information are the unfiltered ones
test.purpose: Stated as an equality between two runs rather than left to two hand-counted tables: the figures reported for an image carrying no line information are the figures reported before this phase existed.

test.name: HLR-154: at -O2 an uncovered file is still untouched
test.purpose: The invariant that holds whatever the optimiser did, and the one the phase is unsafe without: coverage governs pruning, so a file the mapping never described loses nothing at any optimisation level, every function is still reported, and the file is still counted uncovered.

test.name: HLR-154: at -O2 the optimiser prunes more than the source excluded
test.purpose: The limit HLR-154 states, demonstrated rather than described: at -O2 the compiler folds a whole call to a constant and emits nothing for the function's body, so lines the source plainly holds are pruned with the ones the directive excluded. No exact figure is asserted, since one would pin the fixture to a single compiler's optimiser rather than to a requirement.

test.name: LLR-DWL-02: a path with .. components still resolves to the file
test.purpose: The compiler records the file name as the command line spelled it, joined to the unit's compilation directory, so an ordinary build records a name carrying `.` and `..`. The image's spelling and elc's canonical path meet only if the join is normalised — lexically, never through `realpath(3)`, which would stat every path the image happens to name. Coverage is established despite the components, and the guarded region is pruned, which it could not be from an uncovered file.

test.name: HLR-155: the counts survive a record round trip
test.purpose: Neither count can be recomputed from a record: regeneration has no image, and no debug information to read from one.

test.name: HLR-140: with no image nothing is filtered and no section is added
test.purpose: The opt-in promise, and the cheapest regression test available. An empty section is not nothing, so the uniform-composition rule gives way here and the filter sections are absent entirely.

test.name: HLR-140: an unfiltered run is byte-identical across formats and runs
test.purpose: Two unfiltered runs over one tree produce the same bytes, so nothing the option added reaches a run that did not ask for it.

test.name: HLR-143: the source functions the image does not define are listed
test.purpose: The finding the option exists to produce: both functions of the translation unit the link never included, named.

test.name: HLR-193: debug information places each definition in its own file
test.purpose: Two translation units define a static helper and both survive the link; each is retained against the file that defines it rather than both against whichever the filter matched first.

test.name: HLR-193: a definition the link dropped is absent, its namesake retained
test.purpose: The case name-only matching gets wrong: one of two same-named statics is linked and the other is not. The linked one is retained and the dropped one reported absent, where before both were retained and one of them falsely.

test.name: HLR-193: an unplaceable ambiguous name fails the run
test.purpose: Two definitions and no debug information: nothing available says which the link kept, so the run exits with a usage failure rather than guessing.

test.name: HLR-193: the diagnostic names both files, the image, and the remedy
test.purpose: A reader who cannot reproduce the tree needs the function, both files, the image, and what to do — rebuild it with debug information — rather than a statement that something was ambiguous.

test.name: HLR-193: no report is produced when the run fails
test.purpose: Nothing reaches the results stream. A filtered figure resting on a guess is indistinguishable from a correct one, which is what makes it worse than no figure at all.

test.name: HLR-141: an unambiguous run still needs no debug information
test.purpose: The failure is confined to the ambiguous case: with every name defined once, an image built without debug information filters exactly as it did before HLR-193, so debug information remains not required.

test.name: HLR-184: the absent-function table is the last section of the report
test.purpose: The functions a linked image does not define close the report, after every other section, while the image itself stays among the summary tiers above the figures it qualifies. It is the longest table a filtered run produces and answers a question asked after reading the report rather than one the report is read to answer.

test.name: HLR-143: an absent function is located, not merely named
test.purpose: The reader's next action is to open the file, so a name with no line is a finding they cannot act on.

test.name: HLR-143: the report is not a dead-code claim about the call graph
test.purpose: Two lists, two claims. A function the linker discarded is observed; an unreachable function is inferred from a traversal. The reachability section is untouched by the filter and still states its own omission.

test.name: LLR-ELF-02: a function the image only imports is not one it defines
test.purpose: The image carries a printf of function type whose section index is `SHN_UNDEF`. Without the definedness test a source definition of printf would be retained, and the filter would keep code the build never compiled.

test.name: HLR-144: a call whose target was filtered out is unresolved
test.purpose: The callee is in the image's import list and not its definitions, so the call resolves to nothing. Inventing the edge would make the reachability claim unsound in the one direction it is not already known to err.

test.name: LLR-ANL-52: a filtered function contributes no fact of any kind
test.purpose: An omitted function is in no graph-derived table either: not a node, not a fan-out row, not a decision point on anything.

test.name: HLR-145: file-scope ELOC is retained and reported separately
test.purpose: Two lines of file-scope data across the two files, reported as a figure of their own — the part of the total the filter did not narrow.

test.name: HLR-145: a file the image kept nothing from still reports its data
test.purpose: A file with no function left reports its one line of file-scope ELOC, so a reader can tell a file of retained functions from a file of retained data.

test.name: HLR-142: a C++ image matches through Itanium demangling
test.purpose: Every name but main reaches the image encoded and qualified. Matching raw linkage names would retain nothing at all, and matching a demangled one without reducing it would match nothing either.

test.name: HLR-143: a name in a scheme this build cannot decode is counted
test.purpose: A v0-mangled symbol linked into an otherwise ordinary image raises the unresolved count by one and leaves the rest of the filter working: one symbol resolved to nothing, not the image.

test.name: HLR-146: a stripped image is fatal and diagnosed as its own case
test.purpose: The case that most needs to be fatal. An empty function set would filter every function away and report a project containing none — confidently wrong, and indistinguishable from a correct result.

test.name: HLR-146: a file that is not an object file is fatal
test.purpose: A source file named where an image was meant ends the run with a diagnostic naming it and no report.

test.name: HLR-146: an absent image is fatal and names the path
test.purpose: The user named the file, so the failure is theirs to correct and the diagnostic says which file.

test.name: HLR-146: an unusable image ends the run before anything is measured
test.purpose: Fatal before discovery, not after a walk whose results are then thrown away: nothing about the source tree reaches stderr either.

test.name: HLR-147: the report names the image it was filtered by
test.purpose: A report that filtered and did not say which image it filtered by cannot be checked against the build it claims to describe.

test.name: HLR-147: --elf with --from-xml is a usage error
test.purpose: The filter is applied when a file is measured, so a record already describes one filtered run. Rejected rather than silently ignored, the same rule a definition gets.

test.name: HLR-147: a report regenerated from the record is byte-identical
test.purpose: A record written from a filtered run regenerates into the same Markdown the direct run produced, filter sections included.

test.name: HLR-147: the record carries the image and both mismatch counts
test.purpose: The image element and one absent element per function the image lacks, in a well-formed document. Without them a regenerated report would describe a filtered run while naming no filter.

test.name: HLR-140: an unfiltered record carries no image element
test.purpose: An unfiltered run writes exactly the record it wrote before the option existed.

test.name: HLR-032: two filtered runs over the same tree are byte-identical
test.purpose: Nothing about symbol-table order or query-match order reaches the output, which is what the sorted symbol set and the sorted absent list are for.

test.name: LLR-ANL-58: a function no configuration builds is not one the image lacks
test.purpose: The ordering the three exclusions are gathered in. A function inside a constant condition is gone before the image is consulted, so it is not reported as one the linker discarded; a function the image genuinely lacks is reported in the same run, so the case cannot pass by reporting nothing at all.

test.name: the hand-counted totals match with no definitions
test.purpose: Nine functions, nine ELOC, five undecided regions, against a table worked out by hand. Every function holds exactly one statement so the second column can be checked against the first.

test.name: HLR-132: -DFEATURE measures the configuration in which it is defined
test.purpose: The consequence survives and the alternative goes, and the figures are those of that configuration rather than of the union of both.

test.name: HLR-132: a definition can make a condition false as well as true
test.purpose: `#ifndef LEAN` with `-DLEAN`: the symbol is defined, the negation makes the condition false, and the consequence goes. A rule that only ever pruned `#else` branches would pass every other case and fail this one.

test.name: HLR-132: two definitions compose
test.purpose: Two regions decided independently in one run, with the undecided count falling by exactly the two that were settled.

test.name: HLR-131: #if 0 prunes with no definitions supplied
test.purpose: The one place the opt-in rule does not read literally, and deliberately: a constant condition is the same in every configuration, so it needs no configuration to decide. This is the Phase 3 judgement in doc/notes.md §3 reversed.

test.name: HLR-133: a symbol no -D mentions leaves both branches counted
test.purpose: Undecidable rather than false. A build may define the symbol in a header elc never sees, so both branches stay.

test.name: HLR-133: an undecidable condition is counted, not silently kept
test.purpose: Leaving the region active is the safe direction; leaving it unreported would hide how incomplete the pruning was, and the count is the only thing that says.

test.name: HLR-133: a region inside an uncompiled region is not counted undecided
test.purpose: A region nobody builds has no condition worth reporting. Counting it would inflate the one figure a reader uses to judge the pruning, which is the case a naive implementation gets wrong.

test.name: HLR-131: defining a symbol the tree never mentions changes nothing
test.purpose: The narrow form of the opt-in guarantee, asserted directly rather than inferred from the rest of the suite passing.

test.name: the alternative of a leading #if is the whole rest of the chain
test.purpose: `-DALPHA` decides the head true and the entire `#elif`/`#else` tail goes with it — and the `#elif` inside stops being undecided, so the count falls to zero rather than one.

test.name: an #elif is decided on its own terms when the head is undecided
test.purpose: The head stays counted and unpruned while the `#elif` takes its `#else`. `alpha` survives because `ALPHA` is unknown, not because it is defined.

test.name: an undecided chain keeps every branch
test.purpose: With nothing named, every branch of the chain stays and both conditions are counted.

test.name: HLR-134: a Rust cfg attribute prunes by the same mechanism
test.purpose: `#[cfg(not(feature_b))]` with `-Dfeature_b`: the symbol is known, the negation makes the condition false, and the item goes. No line of src/ changed to support Rust's shape.

test.name: HLR-134: a cfg with no else cannot be pruned by defining its symbol
test.purpose: An attribute has no alternative, so deciding the condition *true* prunes something that does not exist. The asymmetry is the language's rather than elc's, and is pinned so it is not read as a defect later.

test.name: HLR-136: the definitions in force are reported
test.purpose: A report states the configuration it describes, rather than leaving a reader to remember which command produced it.

test.name: HLR-031: the section is emitted with no definitions supplied
test.purpose: "Measured with no definitions" and "measured with these" are different claims, and a reader of a report showing neither could not tell which they had.

test.name: HLR-136: the definitions are reported in a stable order
test.purpose: The order the user typed them in is not a property of the run.

test.name: HLR-056: a configured run survives a record round trip
test.purpose: Byte-identical regeneration of a pruned run, which a record omitting the configuration could not deliver.

test.name: HLR-136: the record names the configuration it describes
test.purpose: Both halves: the definitions in force and how completely they could be applied.

test.name: HLR-063: -D with --from-xml is a usage error
test.purpose: Pruning happens when a file is measured, so a record already describes one configuration and cannot be re-cut into another. Rejected rather than silently ignored.

test.name: HLR-032: two configured runs produce identical output
test.purpose: A configuration changes what is measured, not whether the measurement is repeatable.

test.name: HLR-132: a call inside an uncompiled region is not a call of this build
test.purpose: caller survives and the call inside its `#if 0` does not. A pruning that only removed whole functions would pass every other case in this group and fail this one.

test.name: HLR-132: a decision point inside an uncompiled region is not counted
test.purpose: Complexity describes the build rather than the source, which is the same claim the fan-out case makes about the graph.

test.name: HLR-132: a global access inside an uncompiled region is not a fact
test.purpose: The object is declared outside the region and read only inside it, so this build touches it nowhere and no row describes it.

test.name: LLR-CND-08: a language supplying no conditional query has none
test.purpose: Python ships no `conditionals.scm`, which the contract permits by omission: the file is measured normally and nothing is excluded or counted undecided.

test.name: LLR-CND-08: a definition changes nothing for such a language
test.purpose: A definition supplied against a language with no conditional compilation moves nothing but the section that names it.

test.name: HLR-109: one rule file expresses several independently named rules
test.purpose: Three matches under two identities. A rule's identity is the file's basename plus the capture name, so a fixture with one capture per file could not show it.

test.name: HLR-109: the match count is reported in the heading
test.purpose: The section names how many matched, so an empty one is a result rather than an absence of information.

test.name: HLR-107: a rule's predicate is evaluated, so free is not an allocation
test.purpose: tree-sitter's C library evaluates no predicate. Without elc evaluating the rule's own `#eq?`, the capture matches every call in the file and a rule author's filter is silently discarded — the assertion that a user's rule gets the same treatment as a built-in query.

test.name: HLR-031: the section is emitted even with no rule supplied
test.purpose: An absent section and an empty one are different claims.

test.name: HLR-111: a rule match carries no severity
test.purpose: The absence is the requirement rather than an omission: elc reports what a rule matched and forms no view about whether the rule was worth writing, so there is nothing honest to put in a severity column and there is none.

test.name: HLR-107: a rule in the runtime location is used without being named
test.purpose: Binding by the directory that holds the file, with nothing on the command line.

test.name: HLR-107: what a rule does does not depend on how it arrived
test.purpose: The same query from both provenances produces the same matches; only the identity's first half differs, that being the file's name. What a rule does cannot depend on how it was supplied.

test.name: HLR-108: adding a rule requires no rebuild
test.purpose: Asserted on the binary's mtime rather than on the output, because "no rebuild" is a claim about the executable.

test.name: HLR-116: a broken rule in the runtime location is skipped, not fatal
test.purpose: A malformed runtime component is diagnosed, excluded, and survived, and the report is still produced.

test.name: HLR-116: the same file named on the command line is fatal
test.purpose: The same bytes, the other provenance, the other outcome, and no report written. Two different broken files could not tell a provenance rule from a file-contents one.

test.name: HLR-116: a named rule that does not exist is fatal and names itself
test.purpose: Unreadable fails as uncompilable does, and the diagnostic names the file so the reader knows which one to fix.

test.name: LLR-RLR-03: a rule naming an unavailable language is skipped
test.purpose: What is missing is the module rather than the rule, which is the absence that makes a source file a skip and not a failure.

test.name: HLR-063: --rules without a language is a usage error
test.purpose: A query compiles against one grammar, so an argument naming no language cannot be honoured and is rejected rather than guessed at.

test.name: HLR-110: no rule is discovered from the working directory or target
test.purpose: Decoys in the working directory, in a dotfile directory, and in the analysis target, none of which is read. Asserted by planting them rather than by inspection, so that ignoring the file is what is tested and not merely never looking in that directory.

test.name: HLR-056: rule matches survive a record round trip byte-identically
test.purpose: Every new report section is a new thing for regeneration to lose.

test.name: HLR-054: the record carries each match with its identity
test.purpose: The identity is what the report presents and all a reader of a regenerated report can act on, so it is what the record holds.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs with the same rule produce identical output
test.purpose: Rule loading walks a directory, and a directory yields whatever order the filesystem holds.

test.name: LLR-ANL-47: a directive carries information and does not filter
test.purpose: `#set!` attaches a property to a match rather than filtering it, and the match must survive. An evaluator treating every unrecognised predicate alike would discard it and the rule would silently find nothing.

test.name: LLR-ANL-47: a filter this build cannot apply discards the match
test.purpose: The opposite direction, and the reason it is that way round: a filter the query author wrote and this build cannot honour is a condition nobody applied, and accepting the match would apply that condition's inverse. Under-reporting is the direction every capture in the contract errs in.

test.name: HLR-106: the exported graph matches the expected topology exactly
test.purpose: The emitted GraphML is compared node for node and edge for edge against a file written from the source, so a change in what elc believes about the code appears as a diff rather than as a number nobody questions.

test.name: HLR-106: the export is off unless asked for
test.purpose: No GraphML file appears without the option, whatever the output path.

test.name: HLR-106: no companion is written when the report goes to stdout
test.purpose: Requesting the export while the report goes to standard output writes no file, since there is no output path from which to derive its name.

test.name: LLR-GML-03: the companion is named from the report by substitution
test.purpose: An output of analysis.md yields analysis.graphml and not analysis.md.graphml.

test.name: HLR-085: repeated calls are one edge carrying a call-site count
test.purpose: Two calls from one function to one helper produce a single edge with a count of two, so fan-out is distinct callees.

test.name: HLR-156: fan-in is the in-degree over call edges
test.purpose: The function called from two call sites by one caller reports a fan-in of one — the converse of the rule that makes that caller's fan-out one rather than two.

test.name: HLR-156: a global edge contributes no fan-in
test.purpose: The reader of the shared object reports zero although an edge runs to it from the writer: being read by someone is not being called by them. In-degree over the whole SDG would make it one, and fan-in is banded, so the error would move a finding rather than only a figure.

test.name: HLR-074: a global links its writer to its reader across files
test.purpose: A writer in one file and a reader in another are joined by an edge naming the object, though neither names the other.

test.name: HLR-074: call edges and global edges are distinguishable
test.purpose: The export carries the two kinds separately and never merged, so an analysis can tell coupling through state from coupling through calls.

test.name: HLR-096: a function whose address is taken is marked
test.purpose: A function assigned to a pointer without being called is marked a reachability root, and the function that installs it is not.

test.name: HLR-077: an unresolvable call is counted, not fatal
test.purpose: A library call is counted as unresolved and the run still succeeds.

test.name: HLR-077: the unresolved count reaches the report
test.purpose: The project summary states the count, so a reader can judge the graph's completeness without reading the export.

test.name: HLR-077: no destination is invented for an unresolved call
test.purpose: The edge count is exactly what the fixture header accounts for; a tool guessing at an unresolved target would have more.

test.name: HLR-033: node identifiers follow sorted file order
test.purpose: The exported node order is the sorted-path order of the files, which is not the order a directory walk yields them in.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same tree produce identical GraphML
test.purpose: The export is byte-identical across runs, so no container's internal enumeration reaches the output.

test.name: HLR-075: the graph spans every target argument, not each one alone
test.purpose: Naming the two sources as separate arguments builds the same graph as naming the directory holding them, byte for byte. Identity is the right assertion rather than an over-strong one, since node identifiers run in sorted file order rather than in argument order: a resolver scoping resolution to one target would drop the cross-file edges and count them unresolved instead.

test.name: HLR-075: a cross-target call resolves rather than counting unresolved
test.purpose: The half the identity above cannot see alone: two runs that both resolved nothing across the boundary would still match each other. A global written in one target and read in the other must produce an edge joining nodes the two separate arguments contributed.

test.name: HLR-076: the graph is built without reopening a source file
test.purpose: Each source is opened exactly once under strace while the graph is built, so cross-file resolution uses the facts of the single parse rather than re-reading.

test.name: HLR-168: the planted utility sink is classified as one
test.purpose: Six functions call the fixture's logger and it calls nothing, so its hub score is exactly zero and its authority the highest in the tree — the shape HLR-168 describes, worked out by hand in the fixture header.

test.name: HLR-169: the planted dispatcher is classified as a god object
test.purpose: The highest betweenness and the highest hub score together. Betweenness alone would not separate a monolithic dispatcher from a legitimate waypoint, which is why the requirement asks for both.

test.name: HLR-170: the leaf hanging off the tree is peripheral
test.purpose: A function with one undirected neighbour lies in the first core, outside the mutually connected centre a layering is read from.

test.name: HLR-174: each row names the metric and value that triggered it
test.purpose: The betweenness of 14, the authority of 1.0000, and the coreness of 1 all appear beside the classifications they produced, each matching the figure derived by hand in the fixture header.

test.name: HLR-174: each row names the action taken upon it
test.purpose: Masking a reader cannot inspect is a black box, so each row states what the masking did to the view.

test.name: HLR-168: a utility sink loses its incoming edges and a god object both
test.purpose: Twelve of fifteen call edges, counted edge by edge in the fixture header. The count is the asymmetry made checkable.

test.name: HLR-170: nothing else is classified
test.purpose: Seven of the ten functions are classified as nothing. `main` and `boot` are the sharpest of them: each passes the hub half of the utility-sink test and neither is a sink, so an implementation testing either half alone reports them.

test.name: HLR-167: the masked functions keep the degrees the report gives them
test.purpose: The masked sink still reports the fan-in every one of its six callers gives it, and the masked dispatcher still reports a fan-out of four — the measurements are taken over the graph as built.

test.name: HLR-167: changing a threshold moves no reported measurement
test.purpose: The strongest statement of the containment available from outside: the report is byte-identical across three purification settings but for the purification section itself. An implementation masking the graph in place would differ in the fan-out, the coupling, and the matrix.

test.name: HLR-171: no classification carries a severity or becomes a finding
test.purpose: The Findings section mentions none of the three classes. A classification is an observation about the shape of a graph, not a measurement banded against an accepted range.

test.name: HLR-171: the section names the thresholds as elc's own heuristic
test.purpose: The label is what separates shipping MISRA and Martin values from having invented them, and none of these five is published.

test.name: HLR-171: the five thresholds in force appear in the heading
test.purpose: A classification is not checkable against a threshold the report does not state.

test.name: HLR-170: the core depth is configurable in both directions
test.purpose: A shallower depth keeps the leaf in the view and a deeper one strips everything the centrality tests did not name; both classifications hold either way, because they are asked first.

test.name: HLR-171: the centrality thresholds are configurable
test.purpose: The sink and god-object thresholds are settable and the classifications hold at their strictest, since the planted functions outrank every other in the tree.

test.name: HLR-063: a rank threshold above 100 is a usage error
test.purpose: A percentage of the other functions has a ceiling, and a threshold above it names a position no function can occupy.

test.name: HLR-174: the report goes to the results destination, not to stdout
test.purpose: A run redirecting its report to a file produces nothing on the terminal, the purification section included: HLR-038 reserves that stream.

test.name: HLR-150: the section is a detail tier
test.purpose: One row per classified function, so the partition rule puts it with the other per-entity tables rather than in the summary.

test.name: HLR-031: both human formats present the section
test.purpose: The table and the Markdown report present the same tiers at the same verbosity.

test.name: HLR-054: the record carries the classifications and regenerates them
test.purpose: A record carries the classifications and the thresholds behind them, and a report regenerated from it presents both — regeneration has no graph to recompute a centrality over.

test.name: HLR-179: two runs over the same tree classify identically
test.purpose: HITS is iterative and its scores approximate, so the ordering read off them is the part that has to be pinned rather than assumed.

test.name: HLR-179: the classification does not depend on the order of the targets
test.purpose: The graph is the same graph whichever way its files were reached, so the ranking read off it is too — node identifiers run in the report's sorted file order.

test.name: HLR-172: a plainly layered tree recovers that layering
test.purpose: Three directories whose calls run one way fold into three layers in that order, from the hand-worked topological positions and degrees in README.md.

test.name: HLR-172: one function reaching far down does not drag its directory
test.purpose: A completion callback defined in the service layer and called from the layer beneath it sits last in the order; the service layer stays above the hardware layer, which a fold reading the latest member would not manage.

test.name: HLR-172: an architecture orders directories, not functions
test.purpose: Seven functions, three rows. A proposal listing functions would be a topological order wearing a layering's name.

test.name: HLR-172: a cyclic recovery view reports the cycles instead
test.purpose: A tree whose hardware layer calls back up has no topological ordering, and the mutually reachable groups are reported in place of a layering rather than the graph being ordered arbitrarily.

test.name: HLR-172: a cycle is reported as a set, not as a path
test.purpose: A strongly connected component is a set: the members are listed and no arrow chain asserts a path that may not exist.

test.name: HLR-172: the proposal states what was masked and what excluded
test.purpose: A layering recovered from a graph with parts of it set aside is a claim about that graph, so the heading says how much was set aside before the rows say anything.

test.name: HLR-173: recovering a layering leaves conformance omitted
test.purpose: The case the whole phase turns on. A three-layer architecture is recovered with complete confidence and the conformance analyses are still reported as omitted for want of a declaration — a tool marking its own homework would pass every other case in this group and fail this one.

test.name: HLR-173: the matrix subjects are directories, not recovered layers
test.purpose: The one part of the conformance section a missing declaration does not silence takes its subjects from the directories discovery established, never from the proposal: a matrix whose rows were read off the graph it arranges would make every project look layered.

test.name: HLR-173: the proposal is rendered as arguments
test.purpose: The proposal appears in the form `--stratum` and `--stratum-order` accept, under a heading saying `elc` never applies it.

test.name: HLR-173: the emitted proposal is accepted by elc unmodified
test.purpose: The printed line is passed back through a shell exactly as it was printed and is accepted; the quoting is load-bearing, and nothing is created by a shell reading part of it as a redirection.

test.name: HLR-173: adopting the proposal is what makes it a baseline
test.purpose: Passed back, the same layering becomes the declaration the conformance analyses measure against — and the declaring is the user's.

test.name: HLR-175: the manifest is written beside the report and named from it
test.purpose: The manifest takes its name from the report's output path by extension substitution and carries the format version and the classifications the run made.

test.name: HLR-119: no output path, no manifest
test.purpose: With the report on standard output there is no path to derive a name from, so nothing is written and nothing is said about it.

test.name: HLR-177: a manifest keeping the dispatcher changes the layering
test.purpose: Told to keep the planted god object in the view, `elc` reads a different layering off the graph — which is what makes the manifest worth having.

test.name: HLR-177: the report says which classifications came from the manifest
test.purpose: The row the manifest stated is attributed to it and the rows `elc` computed are attributed to `elc`, so a reader can tell the tool's assumptions from their own team's.

test.name: HLR-177: a manifest naming an unknown function is reported and ignored
test.purpose: A statement naming a function no analysed file defines is reported on stderr and the run succeeds — analysing one directory of a project whose manifest covers all of it is ordinary use.

test.name: HLR-176: a malformed manifest ends the run
test.purpose: A file that is not JSON ends the run with a diagnostic naming the path and the position of the fault, and a fatal exit status.

test.name: HLR-176: well-formed JSON that is not a manifest ends the run too
test.purpose: Three files that parse and are not manifests — no version, an unknown class name, a version from a later build — each end the run the same way, because well-formedness is Jansson's judgement and being a manifest is `elc`'s.

test.name: HLR-176: a manifest that is not named is not read
test.purpose: Manifests planted in the working directory, in an ancestor, and in the target under every name a tool might look for produce output byte-identical to their absence.

test.name: HLR-175: a written manifest is accepted back unmodified
test.purpose: The round trip end to end: the file `elc` wrote is handed back and every classification it names is then attributed to it, with the masking it recorded in force.

test.name: HLR-178: the two drawings are written beside the report
test.purpose: Both are written, named from the report's own path, and neither replaces the annotated call tree, which is written beside them.

test.name: HLR-178: a masked node is drawn detached rather than deleted
test.purpose: The masked function is present in the purified drawing, greyed, labelled with its class and holding no edge; the raw drawing beside it carries all fifteen call edges and no classification, and the purified one the three that survived.

test.name: HLR-119: no output path, no drawings
test.purpose: With the report on standard output neither drawing is written, by the rule every companion follows.

test.name: HLR-150: the recovery section is a detail tier
test.purpose: One row per directory, so the partition rule puts the section with the other per-entity tables rather than in the summary.

test.name: HLR-031: both human formats present the recovered layering
test.purpose: The tier reaches the aligned table and the Markdown alike, which the shared traversal is what guarantees.

test.name: HLR-054: the record carries the proposal and regenerates it
test.purpose: The record holds the recovery element, and a report regenerated from it presents the same proposal and the same omitted conformance analyses — restored, never re-derived, and never read back as a declaration.

test.name: HLR-179: two runs over the same tree propose one layering
test.purpose: Two runs over one tree produce byte-identical reports, so neither the ordering underneath nor the fold above it carries an enumeration order into the output.

test.name: HLR-038: the recovery section goes to the results destination
test.purpose: A run redirecting its report to a file produces nothing on the terminal, the recovery section included.

test.name: HLR-002: the repository route yields exactly the tracked source files
test.purpose: The analysed set of a repository target is exactly the tracked, non-binary, non-hidden source files, matching the set counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: the hand-counted repository totals match
test.purpose: The file count and physical line total for the repository target match the values counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: HLR-003: an untracked file is excluded
test.purpose: A perfectly ordinary source file that the filesystem walk would find is absent from the result, its only disqualification being that it is not in the tree at `HEAD`.

test.name: HLR-003: a gitignored build directory is excluded
test.purpose: Generated output under an ignored directory is excluded, which is where a filesystem walk goes wrong by the largest margin.

test.name: HLR-003: .gitignore is never read to decide this
test.purpose: Deleting `.gitignore` changes nothing about the result, so the exclusion follows from what git tracks rather than from elc parsing the ignore rules — which it would then have to keep in agreement with git across nested files, negations, and `core.excludesFile`.

test.name: HLR-003: a tracked file with binary content is excluded despite its extension
test.purpose: A tracked file named `.c` whose content is binary is excluded, and the extension list is shown not to contain `.c`, so git's own content check is what excluded it.

test.name: HLR-005: the exclusions of the filesystem walk apply to this route too
test.purpose: A tracked file with an excluded extension, and tracked hidden entries, are absent from the repository route's result, so the two routes agree about exclusions git is happy to report.

test.name: HLR-126: naming a subdirectory analyses that subdirectory and nothing above it
test.purpose: A subdirectory target yields the files beneath it alone, though the tree at `HEAD` is the whole repository.

test.name: HLR-126: the scoped totals are the subdirectory's, not the repository's
test.purpose: The scoped file count and line total differ from the whole repository's, so a missing scope test fails here rather than inflating a figure nobody questions.

test.name: HLR-126: a directory denotes the same files by either route
test.purpose: The same directory enumerated from the repository and then, with the repository removed, traversed from the filesystem, yields the same file set — the property the scoping requirement exists to guarantee, asserted against both routes rather than inferred from one.

test.name: HLR-004: a directory in no repository is walked at the filesystem level
test.purpose: A directory outside any repository reports the filesystem route.

test.name: HLR-002: an enclosing repository that does not track the target is disregarded
test.purpose: A gitignored build directory inside a work tree reports the filesystem route and yields its contents, rather than reporting an empty result indistinguishable from a directory with no source in it.

test.name: HLR-002: a directory tracked by no repository above it falls back
test.purpose: A freshly created directory inside a work tree — the version-controlled home directory reduced to its essential shape — reports the filesystem route and is analysed.

test.name: HLR-002: a repository with no commits falls back rather than failing
test.purpose: A repository whose `HEAD` resolves to nothing is treated as inapplicable rather than as an error, since a freshly initialised repository is an ordinary state.

test.name: HLR-127: the route is reported for each directory target
test.purpose: A run over a repository target and a plain directory reports a Discovery section naming each target with the route applied to it.

test.name: HLR-072: one directory named twice is one row, canonically spelled
test.purpose: Two spellings of one directory produce a single Discovery row naming its canonical path, so the section reports directories rather than arguments and agrees with a Files section that has already collapsed them.

test.name: HLR-033: the discovery section does not depend on the order of the targets
test.purpose: The same two targets in either order produce identical reports, so the Discovery section is ordered by a key rather than by the order the user typed.

test.name: HLR-006: a repository target produces the same report shape as any other
test.purpose: A repository target and a plain directory target produce the same section headings, completing a claim the man page has made since Phase 5 of which only the file and plain-directory halves were tested.

test.name: HLR-056: the record carries the route, so regeneration is the same report
test.purpose: A report regenerated from a record is byte-identical to a direct run, and exactly one line of it names the target with its route — so the routes survived the round trip rather than both reports being equally empty.

test.name: the hand-counted determinism totals match
test.purpose: The file count and physical line total match the values counted by hand in the fixture's header.

test.name: HLR-033: files are presented in byte order, not creation order
test.purpose: The reported paths are in ascending byte order, though the tree was created in a different one.

test.name: HLR-032: two runs over the same target are byte-identical
test.purpose: Repeating an unmodified run over the fixture tree produces identical bytes.

test.name: HLR-033: two directory targets in either order agree
test.purpose: Two overlapping directory targets produce the same report whichever order they are named in.

test.name: HLR-033: a file target and a directory target in either order agree
test.purpose: The independence of target order holds across the two classification routes, not only within one of them.

test.name: HLR-039: decoys in the working directory, the target, and an ancestor change nothing
test.purpose: Configuration-like files planted in all three locations produce output byte-identical to their absence.

test.name: HLR-039: a decoy does not change the file count either
test.purpose: A decoy planted in the target does not appear in the report as a discovered file.

test.name: HLR-040: the binary links no interpreter or virtual machine
test.purpose: The link line is checked against an allowlist; a language runtime appearing there is what the requirement forbids.

test.name: HLR-040: elc makes no network syscall
test.purpose: `strace -e trace=%network` over a full run logs no network syscall. This observes the syscalls directly rather than inferring the property from survival inside an isolated network namespace: it proves `elc` never *attempts* network access, and it runs in containers where unprivileged user namespaces are unavailable.

test.name: HLR-041: /proc reports a single thread while elc runs
test.purpose: The running process reports exactly one thread. Redirecting the report into a FIFO removes the race that made this observation impossible before: opening a FIFO for writing blocks until a reader arrives, so the sample is taken while elc is certainly alive.

test.name: HLR-041: elc issues no thread-creating syscall
test.purpose: No clone or clone3 syscall is observed for the whole run, which is stronger than sampling a thread count because it holds for every instant rather than the one sampled.

test.name: HLR-041: elc links no threading library
test.purpose: No threading library appears on the link line.

test.name: LLR-DOT-02: elc links no Graphviz library
test.purpose: Graphviz renders the output; elc writes it. Plain text emission is what keeps Graphviz a tool the user may run on the result rather than a dependency of producing it, and a link check is how that claim stays true.

test.name: LLR-DOT-02: writing the call tree spawns no process
test.purpose: The half a link check cannot make: a real run that writes a call tree issues one execve, the kernel's own, so elc does not shell out to dot either.

test.name: HLR-041: elc references no thread-creation symbol
test.purpose: No thread-creation symbol is referenced by the binary.

test.name: the build's required flags survive an overridden CFLAGS
test.purpose: The language standard, the warning set, and the header-dependency generation all appear in the compile command when CFLAGS is overridden from the command line, so a build invoked with an added flag is compiled under the same rules as one invoked with none.

test.name: HLR-041: the build passes no threading flag
test.purpose: The build never passes -pthread, which would silently license a future thread.

test.name: the help block and the real target set agree
test.purpose: Every declared target appears in the makefile's help block and every name in that block is a real target, so the hand-maintained summary cannot drift from what the build actually offers.

test.name: make help prints the block from the file's header
test.purpose: The help target prints the header block itself, marker stripped, so a reader who opens the file and a reader who runs it see one text.

test.name: every grammar is linked with the scanner it requires
test.purpose: No delivered grammar has an unresolved external-scanner symbol. The rule located an optional scanner with a construct make expands before running the recipe, so it looked for a file the fetch above it had not unpacked and silently found none — invisible while C, which has no scanner, was the only grammar.

test.name: the grammar build takes its owner and reference as parameters
test.purpose: The rule for a grammar hosted outside the parsing library's organisation reaches that owner, and fetches by commit rather than by tag because its upstream cuts no releases. Both would be impossible with either value hardcoded.

test.name: every grammar the build declares is one the build can produce
test.purpose: Each name the build lists has a rule behind it. A missing one fails only on a clean tree, which is the tree nobody builds on.

test.name: check-prereqs reports every grammar against upstream
